title: MoE-SpAc: Efficient MoE Inference Based on Speculative Activation Utility in Heterogeneous Edge Scenarios
claim: Autoregressive decoding gives sparse, uninformative signals and idle memory; speculative decoding adds reuse and lookahead, enabling parallel scheduling.
layout: 2 rows, top baseline and bottom ours, theory left and timeline right
description: The figure has two stacked rows separated by a dashed line. The top row is Autoregressive Decoding and the bottom row is Speculative Decoding (Ours). Each row has a left half and a right half. The left half shows token steps with the experts each step activates. An arrow leads to a six-cell expert activation map (E1–E6). Autoregressive cells are binary 0/1. Speculative cells hold counts such as 2, 1, 3, so the expert reuse becomes an information gain. The right half is a memory and compute timeline. In autoregressive decoding, long pink cached-idle blocks sit between short green active blocks. In speculative decoding, memory is freed and experts are prefetched during drafting, with darker green blocks for reused experts. Two dashed legend boxes sit at the bottom. Teal, green and pink carry the meaning.
caption: Two key observations how speculative decoding (SD, Bottom) better benefits MoE inference than autoregressive decoding (AR, Top). Theoretically (Left), SD enables expert reuse and transforms activation utility signals from AR into informative frequency-valued ones. Practically (Right), experts can be scheduled in parallel by proactively leaving more memory for experts to come and asynchronously prefetching experts during the drafting phase.
abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models enable scalable performance but face severe memory constraints on edge devices. Existing offloading strategies struggle with I/O bottlenecks due to the dynamic, low-information nature of autoregressive expert activation. In this paper, we propose to repurpose Speculative Decoding (SD) not merely as a compute accelerator, but as an informative lookahead sensor for memory management, supported by our theoretical and empirical analyses. Hence, we introduce MoE-SpAc, an MoE inference framework that integrates a Speculative Utility Estimator to track expert demand, a Heterogeneous Workload Balancer to dynamically partition computation via online integer optimization, and an Asynchronous Execution Engine to unify the prefetching and eviction in the same utility space. Extensive experiments on seven benchmarks demonstrate that MoE-SpAc achieves a 42% improvement in TPS over the SOTA SD-based baseline, and an average 4.04x speedup over all standard baselines. Code is available at https://github.com/lshAlgorithm/MoE-SpAc .
